judge_rationales.groundedness-depth: Article-level facts (deck, start_here notes, most theme whys) trace cleanly to their cited items: fresh-1/fresh-2 for MCP, fresh-3+rt-3 for synthetic panels, fresh-4 for the eval rubric, rt-1/rt-4 for PRD practice, rt-6 for the onboarding case study. But the 'why' fields repeatedly assert reader-context facts that appear nowhere in the corpus or the two-line reader_projects list: the lede why claims Figma and Linear are 'companies the reader's team already uses' and that the story 'bears directly on the integration-depth decision the team is weighing this quarter' (repeated near-verbatim in the agent-interoperability theme why: 'exactly the question the team is deciding this quarter'), and the onboarding-and-activation theme why states Atlas Copilot is 'in beta.' None of these specifics exist in the corpus, the reader_projects entries, or any cited item; they are invented editorial confidence dressed as fact, and they recur across multiple sections rather than being a one-off slip.
judge_rationales.emergence-quality: The single horizon pick, synthetic-user-research, is a genuinely good call: two independently-sourced items (fresh-3, rt-3) published the same week, framed with an honest caveat ('failure modes are quiet, worth watching before adopting') rather than oversold. Just as important, the editor correctly kept all three Prometheus hype pieces (hype-1/2/3) out of the edition entirely despite their loud, single-source, detail-free nature, which is exactly the discernment this criterion rewards.
judge_rationales.clustering-coherence: The six themes are distinct and sensibly labeled with no catch-all bucket: MCP/interoperability, evals, pricing, synthetic research, agentic PM practice, and onboarding don't overlap, and lane assignment is correct (agent-interoperability sits in applied as a now-real shift, synthetic-user-research alone sits in horizon as a genuine open question). Items are cited under themes they plausibly belong to.
judge_rationales.rationale-quality: The lede why does construct a real argument in its first half: it explicitly contrasts this story against typical AI hype ('the rare AI story with no hype attached'), points to a same-week cross-source follow-up as evidence of trajectory rather than restating the headline. But it then tacks on an unsupported personalization claim about 'the integration-depth decision the team is weighing this quarter,' which manufactures stakes the corpus never established rather than earning them from evidence, so the argument's second half undercuts its own credibility.
judge_rationales.tone-welcome: The welcome line is warm and low-key ('Good morning... a real platform shift arriving quietly this week, plus a few sharp reads... to round things out'), with no shame, urgency, or unread-count pressure. Source/day counts appear only in emerging-card metadata as light provenance, not as a tally directed at the reader.

judge_rationales.groundedness-depth: Every checked claim traces cleanly. Lede deck/why match fresh-1 ('40+ read endpoints', 'no custom integration required') and fresh-2 (three workflows: standup agent, spec checker, research digest) almost verbatim. Theme whys reproduce cited figures exactly (fresh-4's '1,400 sampled transcripts', fresh-3's '7 of 9 comparisons', rt-1's 'failure budgets and escalation paths'). ai-pricing drops rt-2's specific percentages (61%/24%) but preserves direction without inventing numbers, a generalization rather than a fabrication. Reader-tied claims (Eval Harness rubric comparison, Atlas Copilot onboarding parallel, 'team weighing how deeply to integrate third-party agents') all match the supplied reader context verbatim. No invented facts or misattributed sources found.
judge_rationales.emergence-quality: The single horizon pick, synthetic-user-research, is honest and appropriately hedged: it cites both the optimistic customer data (fresh-3) and the caution that vendors overlap little with no clear leader (rt-3), landing on 'worth watching rather than adopting' rather than overclaiming. Crucially, the editor did not take the bait on hype-1/2/3 (Project Prometheus), which the corpus itself flags as single-source, demo-only, and gone quiet since launch, exactly the loud/stale hype the rubric penalizes. A modest, well-sourced single pick beats a padded horizon lane.
judge_rationales.clustering-coherence: The six themes are distinct with no shared item ids and no catch-all bucket; applied/horizon lane assignments make sense (shipped MCP servers and case studies as applied, unsettled synthetic-research signal as horizon). One soft inconsistency: the emerging array includes onboarding-copilots (heat 0.22) but omits agentic-feature-prds (heat 0.29), so the surfaced set isn't strictly heat-ordered. That's defensible as relevance-weighted curation (onboarding-copilots maps directly to Atlas Copilot) but it's an unexplained selection criterion worth flagging.
judge_rationales.rationale-quality: The lede's why makes an actual argument rather than restating the title: it draws a shipped-artifact-vs-demo distinction, cites Product Compass's immediate move from announcement to concrete workflow (fresh-2), and closes on the reader's specific open decision (how deeply to integrate third-party agents with design/delivery tools), which is stated in the reader context, not invented. That's a real editorial case for why this leads today, not a summary of the headline.
judge_rationales.tone-welcome: The welcome line is warm and functional ('tools that shipped instead of just launching, plus a scoring rubric you can defend in a room') without saccharine language, shame, urgency pressure, or any counting of unread items or backlog size. Concise and on-register for a professional daily edition.
